title: Vesuvius Challenge 2023: machine-learning ink detection reads over 2,000 characters from unopened Herculaneum scroll PHerc.Paris.4
summary: ML ink detection let contestants read 2,000+ characters of a sealed Herculaneum scroll; papyrologists confirmed the text (Feb 2024).
account: On 12 October 2023 the Vesuvius Challenge announced that contestant Luke Farritor, a 21-year-old student, had read ΠΟΡΦΥΡΑϹ (“purple”) inside the unopened Herculaneum scroll PHerc.Paris.4. He used a machine-learning model trained on the “crackle” pattern of ink visible in X-ray computed tomography (CT) scans. On 5 February 2024 the organizers gave the $700,000 grand prize to Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger. Their TimeSformer-based ink-detection models recovered 15 columns and more than 2,000 characters of Greek text. Papyrologists Federica Nicolardi, Richard Janko and Robert Fowler reviewed the passages, which discuss pleasure, food and music and are probably by Philodemus. The University of Kentucky, whose virtual-unwrapping software underlies the contest, called the result a new, readable Herculaneum text.
purpose: Built to detect ink in X-ray CT scans of carbonized Herculaneum papyri so that the text can be read. This benefit was that purpose.
system: Vesuvius Challenge grand-prize ink-detection models (TimeSformer-based ensemble) applied to virtually unwrapped CT segments
model_version: 2023 grand-prize submission (TimeSformer-based architecture combined with multiple model architectures)
developer: Youssef Nader, Luke Farritor and Julian Schilliger (contestants)
deployer: Vesuvius Challenge (co-founded by Brent Seales, University of Kentucky)

ratings.reason: Nader, Farritor and Schilliger shared a $700,000 prize announced by the organizers on 5 February 2024. Farritor had earlier won the First Letters prize for the first word.
The University of Kentucky program behind the virtual unwrapping, described by Seales as a 20-year dream, was validated with a readable text.
A previously unknown Greek philosophical text became readable. Nature reports that the method paves the way to deciphering the rest of the scrolls.

ai_role.statement: The contestants' ink-detection models produced the ink images from which papyrologists read the text. The ink is not visible in the raw CT data. Virtual unwrapping (non-AI) was a necessary precondition. The readings were validated by an independent papyrological review organized by the contest.

must_hold: Ink must produce a detectable texture or density signal in the CT data
Segmentation must be accurate enough to preserve letter order
Readings must be confirmed by papyrologists, not only by model output

echoes.setting: PHerc. 172 (Bodleian Libraries, Oxford), scanned at Diamond Light Source in July 2024; machine-learning ink detection revealed columns of text including the word διατροπή

First Title Prize: Marcel Roth and Micha Nowak read the end-title of PHerc. 172; a papyrological team led by Federica Nicolardi unanimously read the author as Philodemus and the title as On Vices; the book number is probably 1

headline: ML ink detection reads 2,000+ characters of a Herculaneum scroll
metric: recovered 15 columns and more than 2,000 characters of Greek text

comparator.against: the scroll as it stood before the 2023 contest, with none of its text read
comparator.after: 5% of a scroll; 15 columns of never-before-seen text, more than 2000 characters total
comparator.quote: In 2023 we got from 0% to 5% of a scroll. In 2024 our goal is to go from 5% of one scroll, to 90% of all four scrolls we have scanned, and to lay the foundation to read all 300 scrolls.

later.note: The same AI ink-detection approach was applied to a second scroll, PHerc. 172 at the Bodleian, scanned at Diamond Light Source in July 2024, yielding columns of text including the word διατροπή.
later.quote: One of the first words to be translated was the Ancient Greek διατροπή meaning 'disgust', which appears twice within a few columns of text. Since the scroll was scanned at the Diamond Light Source in Harwell in July 2024, the UK's national synchrotron science facility, the Vesuvius Challenge team have worked with AI to piece together the images and enhance the clarity of the text.
